issues.failure_explanation: The 'only if' direction is false. Take X=R, v=1, f(t)=|t|cos(1/t), f(0)=0 (even, so f(h)-f(0) = -(f(0)-f(-h)) and ||L-C||=||C-R||). Then the expression in (eq:spG) is identically 0, so the specular derivative exists and equals 0, but the forward difference quotient cos(1/h) has no limit, so (H1) fails. The proof's contradiction argument is invalid: it asserts |expr - c| < h from mere existence of a limit (existence only gives < epsilon for h < delta(epsilon)), and it applies tan monotonically to angles 2arctan((c∓h)/||v||) ∓ pi/2 which lie outside (-pi/2,pi/2); the resulting upper and lower bounds coincide (tan has period pi), which would absurdly force the forward quotient to a value determined by c alone.

issues.failure_explanation: Specular gradients are not additive, so the average of the ∇^s f_j is in general not ∇^s f. Example: m=2, f_1(x)=|x|, f_2(x)=x on R; f=max(x,0); ∇^s f_1(0)=0, ∇^s f_2(0)=1, so uniform sampling gives E[∇^s f_ξ(0)]=1/2, whereas ∇^s f(0)=tan(π/8)=√2−1. Hence Algorithm S-SPEG (uniform Random(1,m)) is not an instance of the defined method, and Theorem convergence-of-S-SPEG, whose proof uses the equality, does not cover the algorithm as implemented.
issues.least_adequate_overall_repair: Replace the equality by E[∇^s f_{ξ_k}(x_k) | x_k] ∈ SD f(x_k), which uniform sampling satisfies since each ∇^s f_j ∈ SD f_j (Theorem subgradient) and (1/m)Σ SD f_j ⊂ SD f; the subgradient inequality then gives the needed step in the proof.
issues.overall_effect: The definition of S-SPEG and its convergence guarantee do not apply to the implemented algorithm; the proof step using (eq: stochastic specular gradient method - 1) needs a different justification.

issues.failure_explanation: By (eq: stochastic square summable but not summable step size), h_ℓ depends on the sampled index ξ_ℓ, so E[h_ℓ ∇^s f_{ξ_ℓ}(x_ℓ) | x_ℓ] ≠ h_ℓ E[∇^s f_{ξ_ℓ}(x_ℓ) | x_ℓ]; the proof factors h_ℓ out, which is invalid. The expected update direction E[∇^s f_ξ/||∇^s f_ξ||] need not be a subgradient direction, and the conclusion fails: on R take m=2, f_1(x)=3x, f_2(x)=|x|−3x (convex), f=|x|/2; for x≠0 the normalized component gradients are +1 and −1, so the iteration is a zero-mean random walk with steps ±t_k; with Σ t_k² small (e.g. t_k=0.01/(k+1), x_0=1) the walk stays near 1 with high probability, so E[f(x_k^◇)] does not tend to f(x*)=0, although (H3)–(H5) and the nonvanishing-gradient hypothesis hold.
